title: Advanced Package Workflows: SemVer, Lockfiles, and CI
description: Reason about dependency ranges, reproducible npm installs, scripts and dependency updates in a team repository.
learningOutcomes: Explain dependency ranges versus a locked graph.
Choose npm install, npm ci and npm update appropriately.
Review peer requirements and dependency changes.
Standardize scripts and CI quality gates.

blocks.text: Dependency metadata is part of the project contract

package.json describes direct dependencies, scripts and acceptable version ranges. The lockfile records the resolved dependency graph for the chosen package manager. They work together: changing package.json without a consistent lockfile creates uncertainty, while changing a lockfile without reviewing its diff can bring in unrelated transitive upgrades.

items: `npm install`: installs dependencies and reconciles package metadata/lockfile when declarations change.
`npm ci`: clean automated install from the committed lockfile; requires metadata/lockfile consistency and removes an existing node_modules directory.
`npm update`: intentionally changes resolved packages within allowed ranges; review the lockfile diff and test the resulting graph.
`npm uninstall <name>`: removes a declared package and updates dependency metadata; inspect whether it was direct or transitive first.
`npm run <script>`: runs a named project workflow. Keep documentation and CI aligned with actual package scripts.

steps.title: Ranges express update policy, not the exact dependency graph
steps.explanation: Caret and tilde ranges allow different classes of updates under SemVer rules. The lockfile records the resolved transitive graph.

steps.title: Classify runtime and development dependencies deliberately
steps.explanation: A package belongs in the section appropriate to how the app and deployment actually use it. Do not move dependencies between sections by habit.

steps.title: Make repeatable tasks discoverable
steps.explanation: Named scripts give contributors and CI a shared vocabulary; these are examples, so verify actual script names in the project.

blocks.text: Peer dependencies declare compatibility with a host package such as React. Installation warnings can indicate mismatched major versions; suppressing them blindly may create runtime failures. Before upgrading, check release notes and peer-version ranges, update the lockfile deliberately, then run lint, typecheck, tests and the production build on the resulting commit.

blocks.title: Do not use force as the default conflict resolver
blocks.text: Flags that bypass peer resolution can allow an unsupported package combination to install. Identify the conflicting ranges and choose compatible versions before reaching for a force install.

blocks.prompt: CI needs a clean installation from the committed lockfile and must fail if package metadata and the lockfile disagree. Which command fits?

options.feedback: It performs a clean lockfile-driven install and rejects inconsistent metadata.
Update intentionally changes resolved versions within allowed ranges.

options.text: Delete the lockfile then run npm install
options.feedback: That resolves a fresh dependency tree and undermines reproducibility.
Force can bypass compatibility checks and is not the standard reproducible CI workflow.

blocks.explanation: Use npm ci for CI installs and install/update when deliberately changing dependency resolution.

blocks.title: Review a dependency upgrade like a maintainer
blocks.context: A PR updates a UI library and changes package.json/package-lock.json. Determine whether the change is intentional, compatible and verifiable.
instructions: Inspect both dependency files and classify direct versus transitive changes.
Check the package's supported React peer range and major-version migration notes.
Choose the install command for intentional local dependency changes and for clean CI.
Run or list lint, typecheck, tests and production build gates.
Document the upgrade intent and the behavior tested after the change.
requirements: package.json and the lockfile are reviewed together.
Peer compatibility is checked rather than suppressed by default.
CI installs from the committed lockfile.
Quality gates cover the resulting dependency graph.
The PR explains intent and verification.

hints: One direct update can change many transitive packages.
Resolve peer conflicts deliberately instead of using --force by default.
Run checks after lockfile changes so tested dependencies match the proposed commit.
successCriteria: Intentional and incidental changes are distinguished.
Install commands suit local changes and CI.
A repeatable verification record is provided.

items: package.json describes allowed ranges and scripts; the lockfile records the resolved graph.
Use npm ci for reproducible CI, and install/update when intentionally changing resolution.
Review peer compatibility, transitive changes and tests instead of bypassing conflicts with force flags.
